approachQuestion.prompt:
Entry desk

Each visitor buys one ticket costing 5 units and pays with one bill of value 5, 10 or 20. You start with no bills. Serve visitors in the given order, giving exact change immediately using only bills already received, including the current payment if useful. Return 1 if every visitor can be served and 0 otherwise. Bills cannot be split or borrowed.

Example 1: bills=[5,5,5,10,20] → 1; for 20, return one 10 and one 5.
Example 2: bills=[5,10,10] → 0; no 5 remains for the last visitor.
Example 3: bills=[] → 1.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; every bill is one of 5,10,20. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Count available 5 and 10 bills. On 5 increment the 5 count. On 10 require and spend one 5, then increment the 10 count. On 20 prefer spending one 10 plus one 5; if unavailable spend three 5 bills; if neither is possible return 0. Do not store 20 bills; return 1 after the scan.
options.feedback: For 10 the only change is one 5. For 20, using one 10 and one 5 preserves two additional 5 bills versus using three 5s. Two 5s can replace a 10 in any future change, while a 10 cannot replace a needed single 5. Thus the preferred change never reduces future feasibility.

options.text: For 20 always use three 5 bills if available, even when a 10 and a 5 are also available.
options.feedback: This can waste the only small change for a later 10. For [5,5,5,5,10,20,10], three-5 change fails on the last bill, whereas 10+5 change succeeds.

options.text: Track only the total value of the cash drawer; accept a payment whenever the drawer total covers the required change.
options.feedback: Total cash does not guarantee the needed denomination. For [5,10,10], before the final visitor the drawer holds a 10 but no 5, so exact change is impossible.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

Prefer one 10 and one 5 for 20 change to preserve two extra 5 bills, which are also needed for future 10 payments. Twenty bills cannot help make the stated smaller change amounts, so retaining them adds no useful state.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Every payment changes only the counts of available 5 and 10 bills.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Each payment executes a fixed number of bill-count tests and updates. A successful full queue takes O(n) time, with only two denomination counts and the loop index as O(1) auxiliary state.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
